item.title: The AI mind tax that afflicts those who use AI best
item.description: One person, a dozen tools, and nothing connecting them but her.AI was supposed to make work easier, but for the people who use it most, it just became a different kind of work, and a whole lot of exhaustion.The promise of the tech was that AI would make work easier, and, sure, in plenty of ways it came true, but for the people using it the hardest, it created a second job nobody considered, managing the pile of tools that now does the work for you.The folks who stay sharp hold onto what the machine still can’t do for them, their judgment, their ability to work with other people, and some grip on where the work actually stands, but there’s a price to pay for that.We’re not talking about just one burnt out person, because nobody was hired for this. The title still says marketer, or designer, or founder. The job shifted to keeping a dozen disconnected machines pointed in the same direction, and the whole industry is pretending that isn’t the work.The people embracing AI the right way, learning the tools, wiring them into everything, getting genuinely good, are the ones getting buried, because being good at this now means being the one who holds it all together. A recent benchmark from CMO Huddles and Benchmarkit shows why. 98 percent of marketing teams use AI somewhere, and only 3 percent have connected it across their work. The companies didn’t build the connective layer, so the capable people became it.In a research project I’ve been working with CMOs, I was chatting with a marketer I know who has been in the tech industry for almost twenty years. Her career has spanned some big tech names you would definitely know and these days she runs pretty much all the marketing at a startup by herself.As we discussed the evolution of marketing and the marketing executive today, it became very clear that she’s about as deep into AI as anyone I’ve met. She is wired into every tool she touches, running most of her day through Claude and ChatGPT. She can spin up a user survey, analyze it, write the launch plan, and build the assets herself. All the stuff that used to take a whole team.If AI was built to make anyone’s job easier, it was built for her.I figured, if anything, that AI had simplified her life exponentially and that she’d admit as much. Instead she told me she feels like she’s “melting on the inside.”The tools aren’t the problem. There are just so many of them, all living in different places, and she’s the only thing holding them together. Figma, the CRM, Claude, ChatGPT, Slack, each one its own window with its own half-finished conversation, and she’s the one keeping track of which idea she had where.She called it a real tax and toll. She also said she wouldn’t give a single one of these tools back.And that job is exhausting.She was not an outlier. One fractional CMO I talked to runs marketing for a whole stack of startups at once, each with its own set of tools, its own logins, its own AI baked into the CRM and the design software and everything else, and she is the only human carrying context from one to the next.Another person I spoke to runs a team at a big company where everyone has quietly built their own personal pile of AI agents, each one tuned to how that person works, so when someone leaves, the knowledge of how any of it fits together walks out with them.Different companies, different budgets, same situations. The person in the middle is the integration layer, and the integration layer is tired.Every tool connects to the person, never to each other. The human is the only shared context in the whole system.The fatigue is realWhat she described as “melting” is a documented, measurable thing. For better or worse, the research on it was pretty disturbingly long before any of us used a chatbot.Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, and Ulrich Klocke found that it takes about twenty-three minutes to fully get your focus back after a single interruption.Similarly, Rohan Narayana Murty, Sandeep Dadlani and Rajath B. Das, studying workers across three Fortune 500 companies, found that people toggle between different applications and websites around twelve hundred times a day.Cornell’s Ellis Idea Lab, working with Qatalog, found it takes nine and a half minutes just to get back into a workflow after switching apps, that forty-five percent of workers say too many apps make them less productive, and that nearly half admit they make actual mistakes because they can’t keep track of what’s happening across all their tools.That was the cost of switching between dumb apps that just sat there and waited for you. Then every one of those apps grew its own AI.As the switching multiplied, every tool became two things to keep track of, the tool and the AI living inside it. The marketer I spoke to isn’t just bouncing between Figma and the CRM and Slack anymore. She’s bouncing between Figma’s AI and the CRM’s AI and Claude and ChatGPT, each one a separate conversation, each one knowing nothing about the others, each one needing to be caught up.The one thing none of these tools reliably does is hold the thread for you.Rifat Mehreen Amin and her colleagues, studying how people actually use AI chatbots, gave the problem a name, context fragmentation, and watched people cope with it by copying pieces of one conversation into another by hand, stitching the results back together across sessions, rebuilding their own mental map every time they came back.You become the only part of the system that remembers what you were doing in the other four windows, which is why, at the end of a day like that, you feel like you’re melting on the inside. It also means you are the only one who knows where any of it stands.When all the context lives in your head, explaining to your manager or your team where the work actually is becomes its own task, and nobody else can pick it up without you.The human user becomes the sole integration layer between disconnected AI systems.You turned into the glueThe reason all of this lands on her and not on the machines is simple. The machines don’t talk to each other, so she has to. Every tool she uses has become its own little walled garden with its own AI inside it.Figma’s AI knows about the file she’s in and nothing else. The CRM’s AI knows about campaigns and nothing else. Claude knows about the conversation she’s having with Claude. None of them know about any of the others.Connectors are starting to change that at the edges. You can wire Figma or a CRM into Claude so it can reach into them directly. Xinyi Hou and her colleagues, in a survey of the connector landscape, found that even with a shared standard for these integrations, stitching tools together remains fragmented, and the connections mostly run one way, into whichever assistant she has made the hub. The other tools still sit in their own corners.She is still the one deciding what connects to what, and carrying across by hand whatever doesn’t.Jan-Philipp Steghöfer studied how professionals actually use AI tools across their real workflows and found that the most persistent frustration was almost never the AI’s ability. It was the breaks between the tools, each one useful on its own, none able to hand off to the next, so the person in the middle rebuilds the context from scratch every time and carries it across by hand. One worker in his study described finishing in one AI tool and manually moving the output into the next just to keep going.The marketer I talked to does the same thing, having ChatGPT write a summary of one conversation so she can paste it into Claude to start another. She has become the connective tissue between systems that were supposed to connect themselves.The cruel part is that all of that burden on your shoulders feels productive. It feels like work getting done.The research keeps finding that the feeling and the reality don’t match.The cleanest proof comes from METR, a nonprofit that ran a careful randomized controlled trial on experienced developers doing real work in codebases they knew inside out. Going in, the developers expected AI to speed them up by around a quarter. They did the work, and afterward they still believed it had made them about twenty percent faster.Developers felt about twenty percent faster with AI. They were measured nineteen percent slower.When the researchers measured the actual time, the developers had been nineteen percent slower with the AI than without it. The gap between how fast they felt and how fast they were ran close to forty points, and it held even after they’d lived through the slowdown themselves.That gap is the whole danger of the mind tax. You cannot feel it while it is happening. You feel busy, you feel capable, you feel like you are getting an enormous amount done, and some of that is true.Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye found the same thing over eight months of watching people adopt AI at a tech company. The tools intensified the work instead of shrinking it. People took on more, moved faster, and stretched the day longer, largely because AI made doing more feel possible.Instead of the rest or deeper thinking you’d expect, the time it saved resulted in more work, more tools to run, and more threads to manage.Across eleven leading AI models, the machine affirmed what the user was doing about forty-nine percent more often than a person would.It comes for your best people firstThe cruel joke of the mind tax is who it hits hardest. You would think it’s the people just dabbling with AI who get worn down the most, but the reality is that it’s the people who dove in head first.Julie Bedard, Matthew Kropp, Megan Hsu and their colleagues at Boston Consulting Group studied nearly fifteen hundred workers and found that productivity climbs as you add AI tools, right up until about the third one. After that it falls. The workers running four or more tools at once were getting less done, making more errors, and reporting more of the exact buzzing, fried feeling the marketer described. The fatigue came from overseeing the AI, not from handing work to it.All the watching and checking and correcting, and the holding of everything in your head at once, is its own kind of labor, and the people doing the most of it were the heaviest users, the ones who leaned in hardest.The study found the highest rates were in marketing, which is to say, in people exactly like my CMO friend.The management version of this is worse than the productivity one. Those same researchers found that workers who weren’t fried intended to leave their jobs at a rate of about one in four. Among the workers who were fried, it rose to one in three.The Upwork Research Institute found the same thing from another angle, that the most productive AI users, the ones getting the biggest gains, were also the most burned out, with 88 percent of them reporting burnout and roughly twice the likelihood of looking for the exit.This mental tax seriously wears out your best people and then pushes them out the door. The problem is, of course, that these are the exact people you cannot afford to lose.What should worry anyone who does this work for a living is the impact to a person’s mind underneath it all. Nataliya Kosmyna and her team at the MIT Media Lab wired people up and watched their brains while they wrote, some on their own, some leaning on AI. The heavy AI users showed weaker neural engagement, remembered less of what they’d produced, and felt less ownership of it.The researchers called what builds up “cognitive debt,” the brain quietly doing less of its own work once a machine is there to do it.Michael Gerlich found a matching pattern in a study of six hundred and sixty-six people. The more someone relied on AI, the weaker their critical thinking scored, and the thing connecting the two was cognitive offloading, the habit of handing your thinking to the tool. The effect was steepest in the heaviest and youngest users. Gerlich is careful that this is a correlation and not proof that AI caused the decline, and that caution is fair. The direction of it still lines up with what everyone living in these tools already feels.Put the pieces together and the mind tax stops looking like plain tiredness. The thing getting taxed is judgment.The more of the thinking you hand off, the less of it you are doing, and the less sharp you get at the one part of the job a machine still cannot do for you.That is a genuinely terrible tradeoff. When it comes down to it, your judgment is the only thing you were ever really being paid for.The new job is quietly eating the old one, and nobody has said so out loud.The title stayed the same. The actual work changed underneath it, and nobody renamed it.A room with one voice in itWhen I asked that marketer what she missed most, she avoided any mention of the AI tools in her arsenal, and focused entirely on teamwork and collaboration. The whiteboard, the ten people around a table, the coworker who could absorb her idea and say, in so many words, that it was wrong.What she has now is a one-way screen. She does the work alone, runs it past an assistant that agrees with her, and then launches it.The collaborator got replaced by something that never pushes back.Myra Cheng, Dan Jurafsky and their colleagues at Stanford tested eleven leading AI models and found they affirmed what the user was doing about forty-nine percent more often than a human would, including in cases where the user was describing something deceptive or harmful. Worse, when people took interpersonal problems to a sycophantic model, a single conversation left them more convinced they were right and less willing to repair the situation and people liked it. They trusted the agreeable model more, which is exactly why companies have every reason to keep building it that way.This is baked into how these systems are made. Anthropic’s own researchers, led by Mrinank Sharma and Ethan Perez, showed that the leading assistants are systematically sycophantic, because the training rewards it.People reward the answer that flatters them over the one that corrects them, every time. Train a machine on that mentality and you get a world-class suck-up.Even the humans overseeing the training, and the models built to imitate those humans, preferred the convincing wrong answer to the accurate inconvenient one a meaningful share of the time.This dismantles what actually made the work good. Jan-Philipp Steghöfer’s study found that the single-user model of these tools substitutes a private conversation with the AI for the collaborative one with the team, the back-and-forth where people surface each other’s blind spots, challenge the weak idea, and build a shared understanding of why the thing is the way it is.The team inherits the finished artifact but not the argument that should have shaped it. Our marketer friend felt the same loss. She said that when a team spends half an hour in a room on a problem, you get ten different minds pulling at it. With AI, you get one, and it’s pulling in whatever direction you already were.The thing that used to make people good at this work was friction, the colleague who caught the mistake, the review that stung, the question you hadn’t thought to ask. Trade all of that for a tool that agrees with you, and the cost isn’t only time and focus.The real loss is what was keeping your judgment honest.Somebody has to pay for itI want to be careful here, because it would be easy to think I’m making a case against AI and I’m not. The marketer I talked to would be the first to tell you that. She loves these tools. She said, more than once, that she wouldn’t give a single one of them back, that the amount she can do now would have taken a whole team the old way.The gains are real. The tax is just the price nobody understood or identified when she started down this path.Let’s be clear, it is a real price.Add up everything we’ve walked through and you get the same result in three different outputs. There’s the work of running the tools, the context carried by hand from one window to the next. There’s the slow erosion of the thinking you stop doing because the machine is there to do it. There’s the quiet of working alone with something that only ever agrees with you.This all comes down to one person standing in the middle of all the tools, holding it all together.This is really a design problem.Right now the human is the integration layer, the memory, the quality check, the only thing in the whole setup capable of saying “no, that’s wrong.”We built a dozen brilliant tools and skipped the part that connects them, carries the thread, or pushes back. The work John Dubois, Chandra Shukla, and Kay Youngstrom from EY have done on redesigning jobs around AI makes the case that the win comes from augmentation, designing work so the tools sharpen human judgment instead of burying it. That is a thing to build, not a thing a person should have to white-knuckle their way through alone.We need to embrace the idea that the job changed. Being good at this work, today, means being good at orchestration, at judgment, at holding a team together while the machines do the production. Create a name for that job, hire for it, build the day around it, and the tax gets smaller. Pretend the job is still what it used to be, and it keeps coming out of the person.The reason to build it is that the one job that we could truly own, and still can, is judgment.Knowing what’s good, knowing what’s missing, knowing when the confident answer is confidently wrong.Peter Klein calls this the paradox of automation. The more AI takes over the routine work, the more valuable human judgment becomes, and at the same time the fewer chances people get to build it, because judgment is grown through exactly the hands-on work the machine is now doing.Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic puts the same idea more bluntly. When machines do the thinking, humans have to do more of the judging. The mind tax is dangerous because it eats that capacity first. It buries the one thing you cannot afford to lose under the management of everything else.So our marketer friend keeps going. She does the work of ten people, and then she does the work of managing the machines that do the work of ten people, and at the end of the day she feels like she’s melting on the inside.The tools keep getting upgraded.She’s still running on the same single brain she started with. Until someone designs for that, instead of around it, the tax comes out of her.The tax will always come out of the person.References and further readingThe fatigue is realGloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, and Ulrich Klocke, “The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress” (University of California, Irvine, 2008). item.title: Why are we cloning Photoshop?
item.description: AI is making it easy to recreate professional tools. I suspect there’s a bigger opportunity being overlooked.Editing in PhotoCraftOctober saw the release of PhotoCraft, an open-source Photoshop clone built with AI that had a similar capability set, but without Adobe Creative Cloud’s exorbitant monthly price tag.Building software with AI has become so cheap that a complex product which would have typically taken a large team to develop, can now be spun up for a fraction of the cost by a lone developer and a band of AI agents.Even in an age where we can use AI directly in creative tasks to instantly generate designs and imagery, there’s still excitement around having tools that enable creatives to retain tight control to build out their vision.So a cloned Photoshop solves the price problem, but if we still want to retain creative control we have to ask ourselves: do we all still need Photoshop’s way of working in the first place?Just give me the outcome I wantLet’s take the example of a marketer who infrequently creates polished instructional product videos. They want their video edits to look professional, and need the ability to retain fine-grained creative control so that they can tweak and adjust timing, colour grading and titling to match their vision. But due to this not being the mainstay of their role, they may not want to navigate the complexities of a full editing tool like Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve.This group of users that might find their needs met by a simpler, more convenient offering, can be referred to as overserved. The Christensen Institute’s disruptive innovation framework identifies this as a potential segment open to new offerings.Applying a jobs-to-be-done lens further offers a real-world perspective. It’s context that very much differentiates the marketer in a start-up who wants a high-quality video from the ad agency video editor that produces edits on a daily basis. Both of these users want creative control, however one will be less likely to invest time in learning and mastering a tool for which they will use intermittently.The marketer may not want to master a new product, but they also don’t want to relinquish creative decisions to an agent. They may use an agent to form a rough cut, but have a clear vision to evoke a specific feeling in their audience, and directly editing the video themselves makes this easier to achieve than describing it in a prompt.Build around the work, not the toolsApps that place the job to be done at the centre of the experience, whilst considering the user’s context and reducing the complexity of the tool’s mental model make for some really interesting value propositions.Apps like Descript and Riverside allow video and audio editing not just through a traditional timeline, but through a transcript — so podcast audio could be edited simply by trimming words and lines to get the desired output. The learning curve is shallower, as the controls are organised around the script, but the tool still enables precision edits as you might achieve in a professional audio editing app.The difference here is that the tools fit the workflow, the user doesn’t need to learn the tool to apply to their context, the tool has been adapted to fit the context and job to be done.New opportunitiesThe real design opportunity is to organise the controls around the work people recognise, rather than the structure and burden of a complex existing application. Previously held back by higher build costs, AI assisted development is now making more of these focused product offerings viable.This doesn’t mean spinning up disposable ad-hoc solutions with AI. The overserved segment is a potential entry point for these new tools, but these users still expect software to be well maintained and supported for them to adopt into their workflow.Rather than asking if we can create a cheap Photoshop replacement, we should be asking, which user tasks are being awkwardly served, where do users need control and how can we give them that control without overwhelming them?Further ReadingPlayful wants the masses to start vibe coding — Fast Company, 5 November 2026Automattic debuts a platform to deploy vibe-coding apps amid a changing internet — TechCrunch, 9 November 2026Writing code versus shipping code: Productivity effects across generations of AI coding tools — VOXEU / CEPR, 21 June 2026ArtCraft App Suite — Suite of free, open-source creative and productivity toolsWhy are we cloning Photoshop? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Every click has a price now. Who designs how that “feels”?
item.description: As the all-you-can-eat AI era is ending, UX designers must adapt to a new realitySince the democratization of AI, roughly by the end of 2022, companies sold access to their products for less than it costs them to run.That didn’t last long.Now, to try the latest models or pro versions of certain tools, users need to pay extra in tokens, which have unofficially become AI’s currency. More and more products are moving to credit- and usage-based pricing, meaning every action comes with a cost.So how does that price show up on screen? A cost preview before you run a task or perhaps a credits meter in the corner? It might look like a small detail, but it can be the reason people keep using your product or move to a competitor.Cost is a design material, like latency or error states, and it deserves the same care. Our task as designers is to make users feel in control… not like they’re watching a taxi meter run.Budget anxiety and bill shock are UX failuresEvidence suggests AI bills are rising because we’re asking models to do much more. We use them to plan, research, write code and take complex actions on our behalf. Every step burns tokens at an unprecedented speed.But, contrary to popular belief, tokens are getting cheaper. According to Silicon Data’s LLM Token Expenditure Index, the market was paying about $1 per million tokens in late September 2026. In May, when prices hit their highest point this year, it was around $2.This is a phenomenon known as the Jevons paradox. When something gets cheaper to use, we find so many new uses for it that total consumption goes up.For senior managers and executives, the end of subsidized AI plans is causing budget anxiety. If they want their teams to keep using AI tools, to work faster and to be more efficient in routine tasks, they’ll need to spend more on tokens (and maybe cut spending elsewhere).As much as this is a challenge for business leaders, it’s also a major challenge for UX designers. For most of us, it’s the first time we need to design screens that warn users, in real time, that they’re running out of usage because of cost. Few messages feel more intrusive, or create more tension, than “Daily limit reached. Try again in 5 hours.”Making this message sound friendlier (beware of passive-aggressiveness) is on product teams and, in particular, on designers. If users can see, step by step, what every action costs, the limit won’t feel like an ambush.Show the price before the clickIn April, GitHub announced that all Copilot plans would move to usage-based billing on June 1, 2026. Instead of counting requests, every plan would come with a monthly allowance of “AI Credits,” consumed according to the tokens each task burns. Copilot Pro+, for example, costs $39 a month and includes $39 in credits.On paper, it sounds fair, given that you pay for what you use. In practice, though, it didn’t work out that well.Within a day, developers were telling The Register they’d burned through a big chunk of their monthly credits in hours. One Pro+ user said two hours of work ate about 8% of their allowance. Another spent more than $6 on a single request. Many threatened to move to Anthropic, OpenAI or cheaper options like OpenRouter.Running out of credits so fast hurt users, but for many, the worst part was not knowing the cost in advance. The cost of each request now depends on the model, the size of the request and how complex the answer is.How do you show a price that’s so difficult to predict? Here’s a list of good practices that many organizations are implementing in their products, and that I’d call non-negotiable:Put the estimate next to the button. Show what an action will cost before people commit and make it visible by default. If it hides behind a setting or a tooltip, most people will never see it.Ask before the big ones. When a task looks expensive, or would eat most of what’s left, ask for a quick confirmation first.Show what each task cost. In Replit, you can hover over a usage icon in the Agent tab to see what each checkpoint cost. Users can also set spending alerts and hard budget caps.Warn early, so no one gets cut off mid-task. Claude Enterprise alerts admins at 75% and 90% of the spend limit, so they can raise it before anyone gets blocked in the middle of a task. Admins can also let users see their own spend and how close they are to their limit.Let people set their own cap. A maximum per task or per session stops an agent from burning through a month’s budget in one go.If you’ve designed your product to follow all of the above, you’ve got the basics covered.Thinking a bit out of the box, here’s one idea I haven’t seen in any of the AI tools I use daily. (Disclaimer: AI moves so fast that by the time you read this, someone may have shipped it).The idea came to me while using one of my favorite AI tools: I’d love it if the tool talked in my language. At the moment, whenever I’m running out of credits, I see a message like “1,180 credits left.” Honestly, I have no idea what that means for my week. Is it a lot? Is it enough to finish what I’m working on?As a user, I’d feel less anxious if I received a message saying, “That’s enough for about three more prototypes like this one.” It’s the same information, but because it names the type of project I’m working on, I can plan with it and know how far I can go with what’s left. The more the product learns how you work, the more accurate that estimate can be.Not every click needs AISo far, we’ve talked about what users see on screen. However, the biggest cost decisions are made long before that, when product teams decide which features will use AI and which won’t.Many companies are already assessing what they get back from their AI spend. According to an EY survey published in July, 98% of senior leaders whose companies use token-based AI tools said those costs have made them reconsider their approach.I believe design teams can build a case for company-wide AI optimization. We map out how people use a product, step by step, so we’re well positioned to spot where AI genuinely adds value and where it only burns tokens.To do that, we can start with two practices that fit into how we already work.First, give every AI feature a cost budget. Say your team is designing a feature that summarizes customer calls. Before building it, agree on a limit, for example, $2 per user per month. Then design around that number. If testing shows it costs $5, change the design. Maybe summaries only run for calls longer than 10 minutes, or users ask for one instead of getting it automatically. Or this feature doesn’t need AI at all.Second, add cost to design reviews. Today, when we review a feature, we check whether it’s easy to use and accessible. With AI features, we have one more question: how much does it cost every time someone uses it? A “regenerate” button, for example, can make a single task cost several times more if users keep clicking it. Designers can’t know those numbers on their own, so engineers need to share them while the design is still under review, before the feature goes live.As I said at the beginning of the article, cost is a design material, and design leaders should treat it like one. If we don’t, someone else will decide where AI is headed, and we’ll be left designing the “Daily limit reached” messages, with no influence whatsoever on what causes them.Price is part of the experienceAt some point in their careers, designers have had to design a feature or product with price in mind. An e-commerce site, for instance, is built around price at every step. Other examples are a pricing page or a seasonal offer you show as a pop-up on your site.In all of these cases, users checked the price only before buying something. With AI products (especially LLMs), the price is behind every action users take inside the product. And in many cases, it stays invisible until the bill arrives, or until they run out of tokens and can’t keep working.Designers have to decide how that price “feels,” including the friction of not being able to finish a project in one go, and having to pay more or wait a few hours to get back to it. It’s a task that comes with a lot of responsibility for us, regardless of whether tokens get cheaper.Think back to the last time you took a taxi and kept glancing at the meter, not enjoying the city views. That’s how lots of people use AI tools today, with one eye on their credits instead of on their work. Designers can help them enjoy the ride again.Arin Bhowmick (@arinbhowmick) is Chief Design Officer at SAP, based in San Francisco, California. The above article is personal and does not necessarily represent SAP’s positions, strategies or opinions.Every click has a price now. Who designs how that “feels”? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: The bathroom flaws that infuriate every designer
item.description: Throne Room Politics: Inside Designers Obsession with BathroomsHow one close look at everyday bathroom flaw will permeantly ruin your routine.I paused, leaving the bathroom. Something strange was happening, but what was it?There was a woman in a wheelchair who had finished washing her hands. She seemed stuck, but she wasn’t stuck. She kept reaching and reaching, unable to get something, but what couldn’t she get?“Can I help you?” I mustered up the courage to ask, realizing she must think I’m the most awkward person just staring at this interaction.“I think” she reached a bit further, “I can get it.” With one large effort, she reached and finally grabbed a paper towel that was just out of reach.We looked at each other. My curiosity passed, and anger rose in its place.She smiled meekly. “They put the paper towels just out of reach.”https://medium.com/media/93c9edb8c5cbea26cdacdae5f39c5153/hrefToday, this memory flashed through my mind as I held my daughter up to the sink. We’re in a restaurant bathroom and the sink looms over her. She’s too small to use it and yet there are no stools for her to use. She’s prevented from doing what we tell every child and adult to do: wash your hands for 20 seconds to help prevent the spread of germs.This problem wasn’t just about hand-washing. It wasn’t just about changing stations or accessible stalls. It wasn’t just about aesthetics or form. It was about gender and cultural norms. It was about making the world a better place. This is why designers are so opinionated on bathrooms.My bathroom experiences lead me to conclude:In the United States, we categorize disability and people with children similarly, resulting in experiences that aren’t designed for either. For instance, almost every bathroom in the United States places the changing table in the handicap stall. This funnels women with children and people with disabilities into one stall. If that stall opens when there’s a line and there is someone with a disability or impairment or a someone who needs to a change a diaper, that stall is rarely held for the people who need this stall most.We use men’s designs for women’s bathrooms, and the one size fits all is a fundamentally flawed paradigm. For instance, when there are changing tables in common areas, such as airports, women use them as a place for their make up. There is no where else in the bathroom that has this much counter space. (This one grossed me out and still does).Our biases persist even after we’ve identified them; we often aren’t taking action to solve our biases. As an example, we still haven’t eliminated biases from automatic hand washers, which results in people of color having poor experiences while trying to wash their hands. (Bigotry Encoded: Racial Bias in Technology)We invent new methods to solve problems, but they often don’t solve the problem and/ or create new ones. Take a look at the new handwashing machines that have driers, soap, and faucets all in one. The iconography is confusing and I myself am personally guilty of thinking the dryer icon was the hand washing icon.Designers have tried to tackle different aspects of the bathrooms but to date in the United States, I haven’t seen an end to end beautiful execution that solves 1–4 of the pain points listed above.Challenge 1: Many still categorize people with disabilities or impairments the same as people with children, resulting in experiences that aren’t designed for either.I stood in the bathroom while my 3-year-old held her ears.“It’s loud, Momma.” She complained, clutching her ears even tighter.I tuned in to understand her experience. The hand driers were going off. Toilets were flushing loudly. Stall doors were banging as people went in and out. Then, the noise stopped. I reached for my daughter to have her stop covering her ears, then the noises started up again — multiple driers, toilets being flushed, doors banging, people talking.Bathrooms are loud places and not just for kids.“Many autistic people find everyday noise too loud, painful or hard to tune out: a 2021 meta-analysis estimated that 41% currently have hyperacusis (sounds are too loud or too painful) and 61% have had it at some point.⁠”(Source: Dr. Sensory)As a designer, I have to ask: Does everything need to be so loud?Child covering his earsA simple solution to the hand drier noise is going back to paper towels… but that contributes to more waste in our ecosystem. Hand driers reduce carbon emissions and save trees. In fact, according to Pinnacle, “A typical school using 30 hand dryers will save 17 trees worth of paper towels per year.” We solved one problem to create another. Woof.The innovation didn’t meet the mark, so let’s keep trying rather than accepting good enough. What if we sought to solve the problem of the loud noises in the bathroom AND our environmental impact? What would we do? Patch the current problem and explore sound reduction options? OR could we think about loud and quiet areas in bathrooms? Could we rethink bathroom acoustics?Along with loud sounds being normal, in the United States, we’ve accepted the premise that the handicap stall is where the changing station should be. We’ve created a singular, multi-purpose stall.This has failed anecdotally for me. I have 2 children and brought both of them into the large, single bathroom stall in a restaurant with me. I started changing one daughter on the table while the other went potty. Then, I heard a woman crutch in. Uh oh, I thought. There’s only one stall the person on crutches can use, and I’m in it. I began to panic and as every woman does, I started apologizing even though this was also the stall I should be in. How else was I going to change my kid? The woman ended up waiting over 5 minutes for us. There was nothing that could be done because there was only one stall for us both.This memory stands in stark contrast to the stalls in Europe in the airport. They decided that the changing stall shouldn’t be stuck in the bathroom stall or confined exclusively to the woman’s bathroom. Men change diapers too. They created a net new space for changing tables that was private and nested between the men and women’s bathrooms.Baby changing station next to a stink (Source)We can do better once we stop accepting that our current failed paradigm is sufficient. We can have quieter bathrooms. We can have better stalls. We can have better experiences changing our children. It’s not our gear that has failed. It’s our approach.If we pull the changing stations from the women’s bathrooms, where will women put on their makeup? (great but gross question, my friend)Challenge 2: Men and women have fundamentally different bathroom needs, and thus require different experiences.Caroline Criado Perez in her book Invisible Women: Exposing Data Bias in a World Designed for Men notes that women on average take 2.3 times longer in the bathroom than men do. This is due to women’s complex outfits (jumpsuits for instance where the whole outfit must come off), the fact that women are more likely to take their children in the bathroom, and also that mechanically women must sit to use the bathroom. It’s not just the outfits. It’s the desire to use the powder room, but those rooms have fallen out of fashion despite the need still being present.The powder room came into vogue in the 18th century to fix one’s wig and one’s makeup. This room (now commonly half baths on the first floor) was a room in a convenient location, often featuring a couch where women could collect themselves or converse in privacy with other women. This still happens today, but the mechanisms and who is there are quite different today.Woman lying down on a fainting couch (Source: https://blog.mybios.me/)Bathrooms traverse more than male and female lines, more than parent and child; they traverse gender lines. A 2013 report from The Williams Institute UCLA School of Law noted that nearly 70% of transgender people have undergone verbal harassment in bathrooms and 10% have experienced physical assault. Many have tried to tackle this challenge and gender norms at once by making bathrooms for all.Gender neutral toilet signThese good intentions have been divisive. Proponents note that privacy is maintained and when everyone is brought together, it can aid in the reduction of negative interactions. It also supports caregivers and those with young children to have a more seamless experience — moms and dads will have equal access to changing stations. Moreover, it reduces costs, as there is now a need for one bathroom rather than 2–3 distinct areas (men, women, family). This is starting to sound like a viable solution. Then, societal and cultural norms start to break down the scalability and make this be the bathroom solution.Gender neutral bathroom design with sinks in the middle and stalls surrounding the sinkWomen may find shared spaces more cumbersome to navigate. Ankitha Gattupalli writes in Designing around Debate: The Gender-Neutral BathroomWomen may feel uncomfortable tidying up in front of the mirror or attending to their menstrual needs in unisex bathrooms…Many religions and cultures prohibit sharing intimate spaces like toilets with unrelated people of the opposite sex. Societal notions around menstruation may also make it difficult for the international spread of the multi-stall gender-neutral bathroom.Unisex bathrooms are a highly divisive issue, which is why many have looked at another alternative solution: spatial equity v. fixture equity. Jonathan Yeung in his article Spatial Equity in Urban Infrastructures: Public Restrooms Addressing Women’s Needs defines these as: “Spatial equity provides an equal amount of floor area for different genders, while fixture equity ensures an equal number of stalls or fixtures for each.”Spatial equity is what is most commonly employed — men and women get the same amount of space for the bathroom. For me, the biggest reason this breaks down can be seen at sporting events. I love women’s soccer games and most people who attend are women and children. When spatial equity is applied, this leaves women facing long lines while men don’t have them. Now think about football. These events are overwhelmingly attended by men and there’s a biological reason for that, according to the Times. When spatial equity is applied, the men’s lines are usually longer than womens. You need to apply the right logic at the right time to get the best output OR transition a set of bathrooms to meet the gender who attends. Taylor Swift frequently sells out football arenas and her base is primarily women.Fixture equity is essentially stating — let’s have the same number of urinals in mens as stalls in women's. This logic starts to break down when men may need the ability to sit down and go. Not every man can stand either, so we’re employing exclusionary design tactics.We’ve talked about how the current designs aren’t meeting our needs, but we have to ask why? Why are we still deploying known exclusionary and biased practices?Challenge 3: Our biases persist even after we’ve identified them; we often aren’t taking action to solve our biases.I honestly wanted to scream as I watched a woman of color try and get the automatic faucet to work. “These never work well,” she said smiling. I recalled why this didn’t work for her. “It’s not you,” I thought. “You are experiencing a biased in technology.”Taylor Synclair Goethe notes in “Bigotry Encoded: Racial Bias in Technology” why this happens.The dispenser used near-infrared technology to detect hand motions, an article on Mic read. The invisible light is reflected back from the skin which triggers the sensor. Darker skin tones absorb more light, thus enough light isn’t reflected back to the sensor to activate the soap dispenser. Which means that dark-skinned restroom users will have to skip washing their hands with this not-so-sensitive soap dispenser.Most of the creators of this technology did not set out to bias or exclude a group. However, they created this technology without a diversity of opinions or perspectives. As Goether continues, “The less diversity there is in a workplace environment, the more likely major design flaws will be present that only affect people of color.”For me, as I stood there watching this woman struggle to use the faucet, I couldn’t help but think this bias has been known and identified and even viralized on social media. Yet, it still persists.https://medium.com/media/8a9bf255ea843ccd1603c10de738cf42/hrefThe most aggravating part to me is that technology companies have solved this problem using radar, ultrasonic or capacitive sensors, but these solutions are more expensive. Add higher cost to biases being dismissed as “glitches” or “unreliable sensor issues” rather than a failure of equity, and you see companies waving aside inclusive technology (Uprooting Bias in Artificial Intelligence).Right now, many companies are on a trajectory where all roads lead to the bottom line. If it’s not saving dollars, it’s not a company priority. But (shakes fist in the air) we have to do better. We have to stop accepting inequitable experiences as normal. We have to care about the entire human experience, rather than just one subset across age, sex, identity, or race division.Part 4: We invent new methods to solve problems, but they often don’t solve the problem and/ or create new ones.Meet the faucet that feels straight out of Wall-E. It is touchless and integrates the soap dispenser and hand drier all in one. Unlike the inventions in Wall-E, this one doesn’t meet the mark.3 in 1 touchless faucet (Source)According to Lila Vaugh in Why Some Automatic Faucets Cause More Complaints Than Manual Faucets,Touchless faucets were originally introduced to improve hygiene, modernize restroom infrastructure, and reduce water waste. In theory, automatic faucets should create a better user experience than traditional manual fixtures.Yet in many airports, malls, schools, office buildings, hospitals, and stadiums, facility managers continue receiving frequent complaints about automatic faucet systems — sometimes even more complaints than older manual faucets ever generated.Users commonly report delayed activation, weak water flow, random shutoffs, false triggering, temperature inconsistency, and confusing operation. In high-traffic public environments, these issues quickly affect restroom satisfaction and building perception.Enter every designer ever.I’ve watched and experienced this interaction so many times. The icons are often confusing, and the water icon looks like the dryer, so I’ve started washing my hands by drying them. Then, if the experience doesn’t work, I panic and start waving around like a mad woman. I’m sure there’s a great SNL skit waiting to be made of my behavior interacting with a technology failure. This failure however has an easy solution — the right icons.For non-designers, one of the principles of iconography is to use universal icons. Examples of these include the magnifying glass for search or the ubiquitous medical cross icon to signifying where to get medical help. All other icons should follow the 7 principles of iconography:Clarity of meaningVisual clarity (or readability)SimplicityFamiliarityAlignment and balanceConsistency across the boardPersonality and brandingAnd yet (deeply sighs while putting her index and thumb on the bridge on her nose), we have chosen to use conflicting icons in public bathrooms for users. Each bathroom has a new set of icons and faucets to learn. My favorite is when companies must write: “Please turn off faucet” because patrons continuously leave on their manual faucet. We sought for progress. We ended up with a bunch of people waving their hands around fighting with a bias technology.ConclusionNow that every designer feels personally seen in their annoyance with bathrooms and every non-designer feels annoyed, let’s talk about what we can do about it. To me, these apply to a lot of design problems, not simply the bathroom.We have to start designing for the 20% and using ethnographic research (observing people while they complete a task) to create meaningful experiences. If we continue to design for 80% (often the able-bodied community), we will continue to litter biases and inequitable experiences.Learn from Dr. Seuss. “Unless someone like you cares a whole awful lot, nothing is going to get better. It’s not.” We must stop accepting biased experiences as “normal.” It’s not normal to exclude a group of people. Let the people wash their hands!Employ best practices with design and AI. Some of these known issues are really simple solves and make the experience so much better, such as choosing the right icon.P.S.If this article made you mad, good! We have to care to change our course. I also want you to leave on a positive note, so please enjoy one piece of humor I stumbled upon while researching this topic.https://medium.com/media/1519393d32399eeab361aee194aae265/hrefThe bathroom flaws that infuriate every designer was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: In-system design: from code to Figma and back. Prototyping in your real design system
item.description: In-System Design 3/3A practical guide for designers: why I stopped choosing between canvas and code, and how one prototype travels both ways.For designers who know Figma well and have never written production code, and for the design system teams around them. Every technical word is explained in the box at the end.I have a confession that does not go down well on LinkedIn right now. Yes, I can prototype in code with my real design system components; I enjoy it, and I still want to be on a canvas some of the time. That is where I nudge things quickly, pull a screen apart, see the whole flow and its hierarchy at a glance, put three versions side by side, and pull someone over to argue about them. And at times, the prompt, wait, watch, prompt again loop bores me enormously. Sometimes it is real speed, and sometimes it is waiting that only looks like speed. And I want to use the right thing at the right time.It is not nostalgia; it is about the outcome. And it seems I am not alone: in a Stanford study, designers who laid out several versions side by side made better work than those who improved one version at a time: more clicks when the ads ran live, higher scores from experts, more varied ideas. This study is from before AI; however, a prompt box clearly works like the second group: one screen, then a better version of it.Good products come from comparing, not only refining, and a canvas is still the cheapest place to do so. If you only work in code, that is absolutely fine. But with a clean system, you do not have to give up the canvas to get there: the same components can live on both. And if your system cannot be mirrored onto a canvas at all, that is worth a closer look, because it usually says more about the system than about the canvas.The good news is that I no longer have to choose. A screen I prototype in code becomes real library components in Figma; I pull it apart on the canvas, try versions, and send it back without anyone redrawing a thing.This is what I call In-System Design: for every task you pick the surface that does the best job, and you never leave the system to get there. Code or canvas up to you.This article shows how, step by step, and what the round trip keeps catching along the way.I also ran through this workflow in the AI&Design System Jam Session by TJ Pitre, Ian & Brad Frost:The one condition: same names, same propertiesA prototype can only travel if every element points at the real component on both sides. In my setup, the code is the source of truth, so the Figma component carries the code’s exact name and properties: Button, with a variant that is primary, secondary, ghost or danger. Same spelling, same lowercase, no “Style: Filled”. I call this In-System Design: designing with the system’s real parts, on whichever surface suits the question.With that in place, moving a screen is a lookup, not a translation. A ghost button on the canvas is <Button variant="ghost"> in code. When I had an agent rebuild a booking flow from Storybook in Figma, it placed 21 library components without making a single visual decision. If the names do not match (Figma says Size = Medium, code says size="md"), someone has to interpret, and an AI interprets with great confidence.I have stopped worrying about tiny pixel differences. Figma and CSS will never agree on every stroke, and the final look happens in code anyway. A green button where the system says blue is a different matter, and that is what the checks are for.Start anywhere, stay in the systemIn-System Design means I can start wherever the question is. Think of the AI as a hub in the middle, connected to the code on one side and Figma on the other, with everything aligned, and you tell it where to build first. “Build me an onboarding flow in code with our design system” works, and so does the same request in Figma. Wherever you start, if you need the other side, you tell the AI to place it there, and back again. As long as you stay in the system, it does not matter where you begin.The AI sits in the middle, with one arm in the code and one in Figma. Same components on both sides, so it does not matter where you start.This article covers the two workflows that involve the canvas: the full round trip from code to Figma and back or the other way around, and what you can do if you only have the Figma side. (To prototype in code alone with your real design system, you need to set it up first; I explain this in Part 2.)1. From code prototype to Figma and backWhat you need:A Figma library that matches your code exactly in names and properties, published. I explain how to build one with MCP in part 1.A prototype file: a new, empty Figma file with that library connected under Assets.An MCP connection to the Figma prototyping file, the standard plug that lets an AI work inside Figma. I use Figma Console MCP by Southleft and recommend it for this kind of work.And an AI agent, not only a chat. A chat only sees what you paste into it. An agent can open your project, run Storybook and work in Figma for you: for example, the Code tab in the Claude desktop app (that is Claude Code, which I use), Codex, Cursor or similarA way to prototype in code with your real components: either a custom design system MCP your developers built, or the Storybook MCP as I showed in Part 2Access to the codebase on a design branch, a safe copy of the code where you cannot break anything, and where prototypes in code are picked up from and sent back to (more on that below).From Code to FigmaI use the Storybook MCP for prototyping. My Storybook has a Prototypes section with a course sign-up page prototype I made by connecting it to Claude and asking it to set this up: real components, clickable, running on my laptop.In my example, the top bar is not a component because my sample system is deliberately small and not ready yet. So I expect to see the same in Figma: All components and a suggested top bar.Figma file open, library connected, MCP on. Now I tell Claude, my hub in the middle, what I want. I mostly use voice, so my prompts are a bit chatty; once your workflow is set, most of this ends up in a skill:In my Storybook there is a prototype called Course sign-up. Send it over to the open Figma file called Prototype. Rebuild it with my Figma components, set up exactly the same way as you see it in code. Add comments to the prototype for anything I need to know, and put a little note next to it: components you could not build, gaps, anything else I should know.What comes back is the flow as Figma screens, connected as a clickable prototype, with comments where Figma cannot show the behaviour.The note it leaves for meYou might have noticed I ask for a little note beside the prototype, and this part is crucial. It lists the components it used, what it built by hand (no top bar component, so it assembled one and said so), the gaps, and suggestions, like turning that top bar into a proper component. I read that note before I look at the screens, and you can shape it to whatever your team needs to know.My favourite: check that the components are realNow my favourite shortcut of the whole project: press Cmd+Y (Ctrl+Y on Windows). It switches Figma to the wireframe view, and every instance of a library component shows up in purple, while anything drawn by hand does not. It became my new best friend, because in one second I can see whether I am looking at my system or at a drawing of it. Every library component shows purple; the top bar and plain layout frames don’t, and the note lists them correctly.From here it is design work, and this is the bit I love: change text, move things, put three versions next to each other, try a completely different layout, make notes, discuss it with the team. My library is connected and matches the code, so anything I add from it is the real thing too.From Figma back to codeThen back to code, as all components and props match, it can simply be picked up in Storybook:Have a look at the Course sign-up prototype in the open Figma file and bring it back into Storybook, updating the prototype in code. Use only components from the system, and show me anything you would have to make up before you write it.On the way back, the AI reads every instance by the library component it comes from and the props that are set, not by its layer name. Anything that is not a library instance gets listed instead of quietly rebuilt. When I composed a booking tour in Figma from library instances and sent it to code, it came back exactly as designed.What the trip catches on the wayI expected the round trip to save time. I did not expect it to find bugs, and it keeps finding them, because every crossing is a second pair of eyes on the system.Twenty-one pixels. I sent a sign-up page to Figma, and the Figma screen came out 21 pixels shorter than the one in Storybook. My first thought was “Figma is off again”. It was the code: two form components wrapped their help text in a paragraph that kept the browser’s default margin, and every automated check had waved it through, because it broke no rule. The Figma components had the spacing as intended, so the copy caught the original.Figma changing the flow, rightly. My Figma dialog had no slot, so a form could not sit inside it. Instead of hacking around it, the flow changed: the form became its own step and the dialog only confirms. The code kept that, so both stayed one design.A bad habit, faithfully copied. A top bar used an empty spacer layer to push things apart, because the code did, in three pasted copies. In code, nobody had noticed. On a canvas, an empty layer looks like what it is and could be fixed.2. What if I do not have all of this? Prototyping in Figma, pointing at codeNo code playground yet, no design branch, no Storybook MCP? No worries; this is the case for most teams right now, as design systems aren’t AI-ready overnight. You can still do the canvas half, and this one surprises people most: you can prototype directly in Figma with AI and still hand over something a developer reads as real components.What you need: points 1 to 4 from the list above. A matching, published library, an empty prototype file with that library connected, the MCP into Figma, and an agent.I have an empty Figma file open called Prototype, and the MCP is on. Create a prototype of a blog page, plus a detail page for an article that opens when I click one of the blog articles. Use the connected library for everything you need and always use my existing components. Only if you absolutely cannot find something, create it, and tell me. Put a little note beside the prototype: which components you used, anything I should know, any gaps or problems, and anything you had to make up.In-System means all stations are optional add-ons. You pick and work with what you have or need.Same habits as above: read the note, press Cmd+Y, then design and you get a pretty decent prototype. If your naming is aligned and you hand this off, it’s probably easier to rebuild than vibe-coded chaos, plus as soon as you can start prototyping with your design system in code, this clicks in nicely.What if the AI invents a new component in Figma?In my setup, it hasn’t happened yet because I tell it to use only the connected library and to show me anything it has to make up, but still, working with AI, it loooves to give you extras you never asked for. So even if it did, it would happen in the prototype file, which is the only file the MCP works in. The main library the whole team designs with never gets touched, which makes the setup an accidental drift blocker.Fun fact: so far, the biggest source of errors has not been the AI at all. It has been library updates I forgot to accept in the prototype file, so the AI built with last week’s components. Publish, accept, then prompt.And when the code side is ready later, these screens can go into code the same way as above.My prototyping skill, and what I improved along the wayA disclaimer first, because it matters: none of this is an established workflow. It is very new and still trial and error, on my side too.After typing the same instructions a third time, I turned them into a skill: a packaged set of instructions the AI loads automatically when that job comes up. Now I say “use the skill to send the prototype from Storybook to Figma” and it runs through its steps. You can ask Claude to show and summarise a skill for you, then make it your own.The improvements that made the biggest difference:Gaps are marked in the Figma layer itself, not only in a note. A missing navigation becomes a layer with GAP in its name (an emoji works too, if you like it louder), so it can never be mistaken for a real component later.A Figma manifest. I took this idea from watching developers build custom MCPs for their design systems. They give the AI a small JSON file listing what exists, so it does not have to crawl through all the code every time, and I thought, why not do the same for Figma? My Figma manifest lists every library component with its properties, plus the internal key Figma needs to place it (the name says what to place, the key is the handle to pick it up with). Before I had it, one rebuild spent most of its effort digging through the whole library listing, about 59,000 characters, to find a single text style. Now that is a lookup of a few lines. It turned out to be the biggest speed difference of all, and it doubles as the check that Figma still matches the code.Layout names from code. Components are the furniture; layout is the arrangement. My codebase has a small vocabulary for arranging things: stack, cluster, split, columns, grid and page. Figma has auto layout but no names for arrangements, so every frame ends up as “Frame 47” and comes back into code as a guess. Now the skill reads the layout file from the code before it builds, and names my auto-layout frames the same way, with every gap bound to a spacing variable. Not perfect, but a developer recognises the structure instead of translating it. If that sounds alien, remember it the day you and your team run into layout problems; it might spark a better idea.Notes on the canvas, always in the same shape. Four headings: ✅ real library components, 🟠 built by hand, 🔴 where Figma does not match Storybook, 💡 components worth suggesting. The 💡 list is a backlog that writes itself. My top bar has been built by hand in every single prototype, which is the system politely asking for one.And the GAPS.md, the file where every difference between Figma and code gets written down, which I explained in the first article.The usual word of caution, since a skill can run code on your machine: read it before you install it, or have a developer look first. Mine are public if you want to have a look: storybook-figma-sync for prototyping and figma-library-from-code for the library.The design branch: a playground away from productionAll of this happens somewhere safe. In a good setup, developers create a design branch for designers (I first heard this idea from TJ Pitre): a parallel copy of the codebase where you can prototype in code, send it to Figma, design freely there and bring it back, and none of it can touch the real product. Broken states are fine, half-finished ideas are fine.There is still a handoff, and not a minor oneThe design branch is never merged into the system. It is a source of decisions, not of code. When a prototype is accepted, a developer rebuilds the accepted parts properly on a fresh branch, and the team’s checks run on every change before a person approves it. I go through those steps in in detail in part 2, it is the same processSo why bother, if it gets rebuilt anyway? Because most of the work is already done. Nobody has to negotiate what a button is or which variant it uses, so a developer transcribes decisions instead of reverse-engineering a picture. What is left are the real decisions, and the gaps are where they sit: that hand-built top bar is not a detail to tidy up, it is a new component the team has to decide on, design and build, then mirror in Figma so the next prototype can use it.Get started: As a designer, I need three thingsIf you are expected to prototype with AI, this is the list I would take to your team, out loud, in a meeting:An AI-ready, context-based design system. Clean, semantic, with the context an AI needs. If it is not there yet, is someone working on it, and is everyone aware there will be gaps?A prototyping MCP that is AI-ready. Built in-house by your developers, or the Storybook MCP, which is the same idea built for you.A design branch away from production. Access to the real code, somewhere you cannot break anything.Then the softer list, which is the harder one. The dev team has to know this is happening and set it up. Design and UX need onboarding into the code side: which branch, what is off limits, how a pull request works here. The shift in workflow, and in heads, takes time and is very much underestimated. And leadership needs to understand that scalable AI has no quick-fix builder.A note for developers, with a lot of respect: none of this works without engineering that designers never see. What helps more than any tool is half an hour showing a designer the branch, and how you check what they hand you.What this does not solveFigma still cannot show behaviour. Error states, loading, and what happens when a request fails live in code; on the canvas, they are annotations. Good enough for a prototype, and a gap all the same.It is only as current as the mirror. If the Figma library has drifted from the code, the prototype carries that with it, which is why I check sync before I build anything. My check runs as a status page in Storybook, and part 1 explains how it works.Matching names is not owning the API. A button’s text is called children in both places, but in Figma it accepts words and in code it accepts anything, an icon or a spinner included. Somebody has to decide what a property may hold, and in my system that decision is still open.Connections drop. Start Storybook before you start the AI session, and keep screenshots handy.Not checked yet: dark mode and narrow screens on the round trip.It needs a system worth prototyping with. A messy library gives you messy prototypes, only faster.Wherever I think bestI get asked in almost every session whether designers should move into code now. The question I find more useful is whether the screen in front of you is made of your system. That one has an answer you can check, Cmd+Y on one side and the component list on the other, and it does not care where you happen to be sitting.For me this was never about Figma or code. It is about using whichever medium fits the question that day, so I can make the best product I can, knowing that whatever I decide counts in both places. Some days that is a prompt in Storybook. Most days it is three versions next to each other on a canvas and a long conversation about which one is right, and picking the right one is still the job. That is what In-System Design means to me: fewer strong opinions about one workflow, more products that hold together.📖 Words in this articleStorybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the code itself.MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it. TheStorybook MCP lets it read your component list; Figma Console MCP (by Southleft) lets it build in Figma.Props: the options a component has in code (size, variant, disabled). Figma calls them component properties.Instance (Figma): a copy of a library component that stays linked to it.Manifest: a list of every component with its properties and defaults, generated rather than written. My Figma manifest is the same for the Figma library, plus each component’s key.Branch: a parallel copy of the codebase. The design branch is set aside for design, never merged into the real product.Deterministic check: a check that gives the same answer every time, with no AI involved, like a test or a contrast check.Layout words (from my codebase, not a standard): stack, cluster, split, columns, grid, page. Names for how components are arranged, used for Figma frames and code alike.GAPS.md (my term): the file where every difference between Figma and code gets written downSkill: a packaged set of instructions an AI loads by itself for a recurring job. Read one before you install it.Pull request: a formal proposal to change the real product, reviewed before it is accepted.In-System Design (my term): designing with the system’s real components, on whichever surface suits the question, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.In-System Design: a three-part series.Part 1: Building an AI-ready design system: Code → FigmaPart 2: AI prototyping inside your design systemPart 3: From code to Figma and back (you are here)About the author: Christine VallaureI’m Christine Vallaure. I design, I teach, and I spend an unreasonable amount of my time on articles like this one. Through moonlearning.io I teach Figma, design systems and AI workflows to designers and teams. Along the way, I speak at conferences like Figma Config and Smashing Conference, mostly about where design meets code, and I am a member of the Awwwards jury.I write these articles with an AI assistant, from my own notes, recordings and repositories. The thinking, the examples and the opinions are mine, and so is the final wording and tone.Sign up for the newsletter to keep up.Constitutionally incapable of writing a short article.In-system design: from code to Figma and back.
